request.prompt: How many commercial humanoid robots exist?

result.text:
There is no single official global census of commercial humanoid robots—manufacturers do not publish uniform deployment totals, and industry counts differ depending on whether you count distinct models/families, units shipped to labs and developers, or units actively working on commercial floors.

However, market audits and manufacturer disclosures paint a clear picture:

Distinct commercial models/families: Industry catalog audits identify roughly 30 to 35 commercially addressable bipedal humanoid robot families on the market. Nearly all (~90%) target industrial work, logistics, or research/developer labs, while only a handful target education or consumer/home use.

Total units shipped (including research & education): The total number of commercial humanoids shipped globally is in the low tens of thousands (roughly 10,000 to 25,000+ units across all makers). Lower-cost research and developer platforms make up the bulk of shipped hardware—for example, Unitree alone has shipped thousands of G1/H1-class units to labs, schools, and early pilots, and Chinese manufacturer AGIBOT reported passing 20,000 total robots produced across its lineup in late 2026.

Active commercial/industrial deployments: Actual revenue-generating deployments on factory and warehouse floors are still much smaller—typically hundreds to a few thousand units across leading players (such as Agility Robotics' Digit, UBTECH's Walker series, Figure's Figure 03, Apptronik's Apollo, and Tesla's internal Optimus pilots), with most companies scaling from dozens of pilot units toward multi-thousand-unit annual production lines.

Why the Numbers Vary So Much

Shipped vs. deployed: A university or startup buying a $12,000–$30,000 developer humanoid (like a Unitree G1 or Booster K1) counts as a shipped commercial unit, even if it spends most of its life in a lab.

Pre-orders vs. delivery: Several home-focused humanoids (such as 1X's NEO or NEURA's 4NE1) have opened pre-orders or reservations while deliveries roll out gradually.

Enterprise-only contracts: High-end industrial humanoids are often leased or sold via custom enterprise contracts rather than list prices, keeping exact fleet counts private.
